title: Lightning Talk: Artifacts That Explain Themselves: Build M... Socheat Sou & Prajakta Kashalkar-Joshi

segments.text: Hi, my name is Sochatzu.
I am a senior DevOps engineer with IBM.
And I work on the IBM Fusion product. So
just to give you a little bit of
background of what our product is is we
have over
40 separate repos each with their own
builds. We're building dozens of times a
day for multiple releases. And one of
the things that makes that complicated
is that we're a fully air-gapped
product, which means in our deployments
all the references to the images have to
be by digest. So our dev and test team
don't have the convenience when they're
when they're working on their systems to
be able to look at what's installed,
look at the build IDs on on the system,
and figure out oh this is the build that
happened today. They all all they have
is the SHA-256 digest to work with.
Which makes it difficult for them to do
their job. They need to we're constantly
getting questions like you know, is our
code in this particular build? Or if the
tester is working on multiple clusters,
are they actually working on the version
that they think they're working on?
So you know,
we did a few things to try and solve
that. The we initially started out by
tracking all this metadata in a Git
repo.
At the end of every build, the build
itself would update a YAML file with all
this tracking data in it. And it was
really useful for us, but non-DevOps
people without the practice of looking
at it and without you know, looking at a
giant wall of YAML, they couldn't really
interpret it. So we were still getting
those same questions. So what we decided
to do was we decided to move that
metadata into container labels instead.
And this made it much more accessible.
One thing we did was we made sure to
prefix our labels with some identifier.
So here is an example, I use ISF, which
is a acronym for our product. And so
anyone with Docker or Podman or Skopeo
can inspect the image
and quickly filter out for the labels
and get some of this data that they
need. And the other benefit by putting
it in the container labels is they don't
have to have it doesn't have to be
running on the cluster. They can just
query it from the the registry
themselves and get the data
that way.
And for us, we got a few immediate
benefits out of it. So, we're an
OpenShift product and for those who
aren't aware, an OpenShift catalog is
just a list of all the images that you
can install from that catalog. And
because we put all the labels in those
images, we can dump out the list of two
different catalogs. So, if we have a
regression on a build, we could take the
broken build and take the working work a
known working build, loop through all
the images in the catalog, compare the
labels, look for get diffs or where um
the commit hashes change, and then we
produce a table like you see there on
the right where for each uh
each operator that has a change diff, we
can then link the developer. Okay,
here's a diff of what changed between
the two builds that we're working with,
and that's really helped with problem
determination. And uh it's very similar
to like get bisect in nature where we
then we can start iterating through that
until we find, you know, where the
regression actually happened.
Um another thing we've done with this is
we've implemented a simple build cache.
So, we do use uh the Docker caching
mechanism where you use the cache from
and you can provide multiple images
where you pull from a remote registry
and it checks to see are the layers
changed, but that's kind of a heavy
process. And our CI/CD pipeline, we get
charged per pipeline minute run. So, for
some of our simpler builds, we do we
just check the the the get commit of the
latest build that we had. And if the get
commit hasn't changed, then we can skip
the build entirely, which then saves us
all the hassle of going all the way
through to the Docker cache, you know,
kicking in and doing its calculations.
The other benefit we saw in DevOps is it
turned our images into portable feature
flags. So, a lot of our automation
revolves around installing the images
that we have. And so now instead of
having these as values in our Jenkins
jobs, we can get some of the the base
values right out of the Docker images
themselves. And so, for example, you can
see a flowchart here on the right uh
depending on the
cat the version being built, um Um, you
know, if it's our patch release versus
our main release that's coming up, we'll
can deploy to different environments.
Um, if it's a hot fix uh release, or if
there's a hot fix image, um, then we can
deploy we can run the hot fix test suite
instead of the full test suite. Um, and
then similarly,
uh we also our product actually installs
a bunch of other products. So, there's
like a a mapping of our product with a
couple of other different ones, and we
if there's a change in that version,
sometimes we'll have to offline mirror
it. So, we can check to see what is the
the version of this product that we're
coupled with, and if this different than
what we've just mirrored, then we can
trigger the mirroring job to mirror it
before we start our the rest of our test
suite.
So, we implemented these labels, you
know, to solve DevOps problems, but it
unexpectedly was helpful to a bunch of
our other teams, too. So, for example,
our security scanning pipeline
automatically creates a bunch of CVEs,
uh and collects a lot of data from the
build itself, and it included our our
container labels. And the security team
ended up building a dashboard to help
the developers manage and visualize
these CVEs, and these labels were
already incorporated in the design. Uh
so, they were able to filter out all the
the images that we had built, and there
was a hot fix flag in there. They
assumed we had put it there for them,
but we put it there for us.
Uh and in their own dashboard, they were
able to filter out all the hot fixes,
cuz that's the images they were
interested in, because those had needed
additional uh set of scanning um
for the their purposes. So, we know we
found this extremely interesting,
especially in this era of AI, where
people are taking logs in bulk, and just
passing it off to other tools. So, the
more data that you put into your um
you know, the more data you can provide,
you're actually enabling other teams to
to do more with their with the things
that they're working on, as well.
So, what are some recommendations we
have for people who are interested in
doing doing this themselves?
You know, definitely take advantage if
your artifacts already support adding
and querying metadata, like Docker
containers, right? That's the the most
obvious.
Uh but other artifact types can be
augmented to support enabling or
embedding metadata. Uh for example, we
our internal builds use we build tar.gz
files for a certain set of builds, and
they're just extracted and incorporated
somewhere else. And we ended up just
scrapping the tar.gz method and just
building them as scratch images as
Docker files. So, the you know, the team
didn't really care that it was tar.gz,
it just didn't make sense to uh at the
when they were initially implemented, it
didn't make sense to them to be a
container image, but we gave them
wrapper code to extract the files out of
a scratch image to serve the same
purpose, and then we got all the
benefits of adding labels to our
containers and all the tracking and and
all that.
Um so, when you do this, consider what
data is intrinsic to your artifacts. Um
you know, because that's the the data
that you want to be adding as your
labels. And work with your other teams,
too, to see what information they might
be interested in to help enable their
own, you know, feature flagging and
automation.
And uh so,
and definitely make it easy to add and
query metadata. So, what we did is we
added wrapper functions in our DevOps
library to make it easy for us to add
labels to our Docker containers. So,
whenever we onboard new repos, it's just
calling a few extra lines. Um so, you
know, all of our images now um whenever
we get new repos to be built, they have
their Docker we have those the same
labels being added to all of them. And
then similarly, we made helper functions
for querying that data. So, other teams
with their automation can use our code,
and they get access to all that data as
well.
Uh you know, just one word of caution.
Uh
you know, it's nice that you can pass
all this extra data to AI, but also, you
know, only expose the data for your
needs um so that but not so much that
it's a security concern. So, I skipped
over this earlier, but here's an example
of the metadata that we provide. And you
notice here that like we don't put in
the actual Git repos, we don't put in
the full build logs, we just put in like
the slug or the ID, and then we use that
information to construct the URLs on our
end. So, it's still useful information,
but it's not so much information that it
exposes anything that could be a
possible security risk.
Uh
and that's it. Thank you.
